newsitem.title: USA: Dayton Hudson could sell more stores.
newsitem.headline: Dayton Hudson could sell more stores.

text.p: Dayton Hudson Corp, which recently agreed to sell four department stores in Texas, said Tuesday it would consider shedding more non-core stores if the price was right.
Dayton Hudson, the nation's fourth-largest retailer, announced plans in August to sell four Marshall Field's stores in Texas -- one to Federated Department Stores Inc and three to Saks Holdings Inc.
Chief Financial Officer Douglas Scovanner said the retailer sold the stores because they were outside the Upper Midwest base of its department store division.
The retailer is parent of Marshall Field's, Dayton's and Hudson's department stores.
Minneapolis-based Dayton Hudson would consider shedding other stores located outside its core markets.
"Yes, we would certainly consider disposition of non-strategic stores if we found willing buyers ready to pay enough to make it worth our while to sell," Scovanner said in an interview.
In addition to the department store division, Dayton Hudson owns discounter Target and California-based Mervyn's.

Mervyn's, the company's troubled chain of 300 moderately priced department stores, has stores in 16 states. Its key markets include California, where it operates about 128 stores, and Texas, home of about 45 Mervyn's outlets.
But the farther away from California Mervyn's gets, the lower its market share becomes, with certain exceptions such as Texas.
In Florida and Georgia, Mervyn's customer base is lower than in California, Scovanner said. But he declined to say whether the company has considered getting rid of those stores.
"We clearly have talked to analysts about the fact that our market shares are lower in Florida and Georgia at Mervyn's than in California," he said. "That's a well-known fact."
Mervyn's has been a drag on Dayton Hudson's results for several years. The chain's operating profit dropped by more than half to $100 million in 1995 from $206 million.

This year, Dayton Hudson unleashed a company cost-cutting program that calls for a $100 million expense reduction over two years at the chain. Mervyn's also has held fewer clearance sales, beefed up merchandise selection and boosted gross margin. Its operating profit climbed to $54 million in the second quarter from $3 million last year, but sales fell.

Business remains soft this quarter. Scovanner said Mervyn's same-store sales, or sales among stores open a year, were at the low end of the company's expectations for a decline in the low-to-mid single digits in percentage terms during September.

Dayton Hudson will release September sales results on Thursday. At Target, sales were expected to be "essentially flat", which is weaker than the company had expected for September, Scovanner said. At the department store division, the company had expected sales to be flat to up slightly, but they wound up being below that.

Still, Dayton Hudson anticipates earnings will be in line or better than analysts' estimates, which call for a profit of $0.34 a share in the third quarter, Scovanner said. For the full year, the retailer still expects to meet or exceed analysts' estimates for earnings of $2.10 a share.
Last year, Dayton Hudson earned $311 million, or $1.30 a share.
Target's sales will improve in October, Scovanner said. And while Mervyn's sales are weak, the division's profit has already improved by more than Dayton Hudson expected.
"Mervyn's financial performance has fully tracked our internal plan," he said.
